582.title: The Lord turned and looked (Luke 22:54–71)
582.hook: at the third denial, Jesus turns and looks at Peter
582.howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial during Holy Week, and tradition links the rooster on some church steeples to Peter's denial and his return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malchus: an ear cut off in the dark, and healed in the middle of an arrest. Your line: no more of this.

They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows, Luke says, afar off: close enough to see, far enough to leave. Someone has kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and Peter sits down with the people around it. A servant girl looks at him a long moment: this man was with him too. Woman, I don't know him. A little later: you're one of them. Man, I'm not. About an hour passes. Then a third person is certain: he's a Galilean, he was with him. Matthew adds that his accent gives him away.

Peter answers: man, I don't know what you're saying. And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Then the line only Luke has, in the King James words: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Luke doesn't say exactly where Jesus is, only that he's close enough to turn and see Peter. Earlier that night, at the table, Jesus told Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not. Now, across a courtyard, one look. Luke doesn't call it angry or sad or kind. He just says the Lord turned and looked, and the look sends Peter out into the night, weeping. Preachers and painters have imagined that look ever since. Some hear it as the opposite of a glare: the look of someone who already knew, already prayed, and still hasn't let go of him. And Peter's tears are the beginning, not the end, of his story. Then the night goes on: the men holding Jesus mock him, blindfold him, hit him, and say, prophesy, who struck you? At daybreak the council asks him, are you the Christ? He answers that if he told them, they wouldn't believe him. A long night, and Luke wants you to remember one moment of it: a man who just failed three times, and the face he saw when he looked up.
screen: `TEARS ARE NOT THE END FOR PETER.`
then, large: `THE LORD TURNED, AND LOOKED UPON PETER.`

Imagine someone who loves you finding out and turning to look at you: it's easy to picture a glare, so try instead a face that already knew, and isn't leaving. If you pray, you can imagine it as the face of Christ.
Galilean. What the third accuser calls Peter by his accent in the high priest's courtyard, just before the rooster crows and Peter denies Jesus a third time.

583.title: Herod's laughter (Luke 23:1–12)
583.hook: sent to Herod, he says nothing, and two enemies become friends that day
583.howItsDone: Churches that follow a three-year cycle of readings hear Luke's account of the trial, Herod's scene included, on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke; some readers connect Jesus's silence with the servant of Isaiah 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Galilean by a courtyard fire, three denials, and one look from Jesus. Your line: the lord looked at peter.

Morning. The council brings Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, with charges that would worry any Roman: he stirs up the nation, forbids paying taxes to Caesar, calls himself a king. Luke's readers have already heard him on taxes: render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Pilate asks one question and announces: "I find no fault in this man." They keep pressing. He started in Galilee, they say. Pilate hears a way out. Galilee belongs to Herod, and Herod happens to be in Jerusalem. Send the problem across town.
screen: `I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.`

segments.voice: This is Herod the tetrarch, ruler of Galilee. Earlier in Luke he's the man who says he beheaded John the Baptist, and Jesus once called him that fox. Herod is thrilled. He'd wanted to see Jesus for a long time, and hoped to see him do a miracle. He fires questions, many words, the King James says. And then: "he answered him nothing." Jesus has talked his whole way through this Gospel, to crowds, to sinners, to Pharisees at dinner, and soon to a thief on a cross. Before this man he goes silent. Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah's servant, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, who opened not his mouth. The chief priests and scribes stand by, accusing him hard. So Herod and his soldiers turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt, laugh at him, dress him in a gorgeous robe like a costume king, and send him back to Pilate. Then a bitter line found in no other Gospel: "And the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves." Two rulers who couldn't stand each other find common ground in a joke at a silent man's expense. Luke doesn't explain the silence. Some readers hear dignity: some questions don't deserve an answer. Others hear refusal: he will not perform for a ruler who only wants a show. Either way, the miracle Herod hoped for never comes.

Think of a place where you get baited, a comment section, a relative who likes to poke, a coworker's jokes, and picture the moment the jab lands: the heat rising, the reply forming. Now let the moment pass, not sulking, not plotting, simply not performing, and breathe through it. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of quiet.
Herod's laughter. The ruler who wanted a miracle got silence, and answered it with mockery and a borrowed robe.
Your line: he answered nothing. Silence, right where Herod wanted a show. See you tomorrow.

584.title: Release Barabbas (Luke 23:13–25)
584.hook: Pilate says three times he finds no fault, and yields to the shouts
584.howItsDone: In some churches the Passion is read aloud on Palm Sunday and Good Friday with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that the shout belongs to everyone in the room rather than to someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's laughter: a ruler who wanted a show, and a man who answered nothing. Your line: he answered nothing.

Pilate has already said it once: I find no fault in this man. He sent Jesus to Herod, and Herod sent him back, still in the gorgeous robe. So it's Pilate's problem again. He calls together the chief priests, the rulers and the people, and gives the Roman governor's verdict. A verdict is supposed to settle things: someone in charge knows the right answer and says it out loud. What happens next is a story about what that answer is worth when the room gets loud, and keeps getting louder.

Pilate says it plainly: I've examined him, and I find no fault in him. Neither did Herod. I'll have him beaten, and let him go. And the crowd cries out, all together: away with this man, release unto us Barabbas. Luke tells us who Barabbas is: a man thrown in prison for an uprising in the city, and for murder. Pilate speaks to them again, wanting to release Jesus. They shout, crucify him. Then, in the King James words: "And he said unto them the third time, Why, what evil hath he done? I have found no cause of death in him: I will therefore chastise him, and let him go." Three times, no fault. Luke counts them so you'll notice. "And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." Not the evidence, not the law: the volume. Pilate releases the man jailed for murder, and hands Jesus over to their will. Two things to hold carefully. First, this is one crowd before Pilate on one morning, with its leaders, not a whole people. Christians in the past used scenes like this to blame the Jewish people for Jesus's death, with terrible results, and churches, the Catholic Church among them, have since formally rejected that reading. The sentence was Rome's, and the cross was a Roman punishment. Second, the man with the power knew the truth, said it three times, and gave it up.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE OF DEATH IN HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of something you know is right or true that you've gone quiet about because people around you are loud: at work, in your family, online, in your own head. Say it to yourself plainly, three times, and notice whether it still feels true; you don't have to fight anyone, just don't hand it over. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness.

Your line: three times, no fault. The truth was known, and the volume won. That's day five hundred eighty-four.

585.title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:26–31)
585.hook: carrying the cross, he stops to comfort weeping women
585.howItsDone: Many Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, stopping at the eighth station to remember Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, release Barabbas: three times no fault, and the loud voices prevailed. Your line: three times, no fault.

A man is coming into the city from the countryside, minding his own business. His name is Simon, from Cyrene, in North Africa. Suddenly soldiers grab him and put a wooden beam on his shoulders, and he's walking behind a condemned man he's never met. That's how Luke starts the road to the cross: with a stranger forced to help. Behind them follows a great crowd, and among them, women, beating their breasts and wailing, the way people mourned the dead. And Jesus, who has barely spoken since the courtyard, stops and turns to them.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE, PULLED FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Beaten through the night, mocked by soldiers, walking to his own execution, he has every reason to be wrapped up in his own pain. And he turns to the people grieving for him and thinks about them. He looks ahead to days of suffering coming for that city, when people will call the childless blessed and ask the mountains to fall on them. Then a proverb, hard to translate and harder to pin down: "For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood is hard to burn; dry wood catches at once. One common reading: if this is what's done to an innocent man now, think how much worse it will be when the times are dry. Scholars debate who the they is and exactly what's meant; the saying doesn't explain itself. Many connect his warning to the Roman siege of Jerusalem a generation later. Only Luke tells this scene: women openly mourning him on the road, and Jesus stopping to speak to them. Later it became part of the Stations of the Cross, the devotion where Christians walk the way to Calvary in fourteen stops; Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem is the eighth. On the worst day of his life, he still turns toward someone else's grief.
screen: then, large: `DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, WEEP NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Name honestly what's hard for you right now, and let it be real. Then, without pushing it away, think of one person near you who is also carrying something, a friend after a breakup, a coworker with a sick parent, a lonely neighbor, and picture one small comfort you could offer from inside your own hard week. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

Your line: weep not for me. Spoken by a man with every reason to think only of himself. Day five hundred eighty-five, done.

586.title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:32–43)
586.hook: he forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying thief
586.carry: they know not what they do
586.howItsDone: On Good Friday some churches hold services on the seven last words of Christ from the cross; the first two are Father, forgive them, and the promise of paradise to the penitent thief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Calvary, and Jesus turning to the daughters of Jerusalem. Your line: weep not for me.

A Persian king's garden. High walls around it, and inside, water running in channels, fruit trees, shade, quiet. Dictionaries trace the word paradise back to an old Persian word for an enclosure like that. It passed into Greek, and in the Greek translation of Genesis it names the garden God planted in Eden. Now set that walled garden beside the ugliest place in the story: the place the King James calls Calvary, and the Greek calls the Skull. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle, a criminal on each side. Today's word comes from the garden, and it is spoken there.

Luke gives two sayings from the cross that no other Gospel has. The first comes as they crucify him, in the King James words: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Then they divide his clothes by casting lots. He's praying for the people doing it, while they're doing it. A careful note: some early copies of Luke don't have this prayer, and others do. The second comes later. The crowd stares, the leaders sneer, the soldiers mock. One of the criminals joins in: aren't you the Christ? Save yourself and us. The other tells him to stop. We deserve this, he says; this man has done nothing wrong. Then he speaks to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." Not save me. Just remember me. And Jesus answers: "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Christians hear in paradise the garden restored, life with God, promised to a man with no time left to earn anything. They read the promise in more than one way. Some hear rest with God right after death, before the final resurrection. Others place the comma after today, I tell you today, and read the promise as future; the old Greek copies had little punctuation, so the comma is a translator's choice. Either way, in Luke the last person Jesus speaks to from the cross, apart from his Father, is a criminal, and he says yes.

587.title: Into your hands (Luke 23:44–56)
587.hook: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit; the women prepare spices
587.carry: even in grief, keep the sabbath
587.tomorrow: why seek the living among the dead?
587.howItsDone: In Compline, the church's night prayer, the words 'into thy hands' are said or sung as the day ends, and on Good Friday the last words from the cross are read and remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paradise, promised to a dying thief, and a prayer for the ones doing the harm. Your line: they know not what they do.

Some prayers are learned so early they're there when nothing else is. At the end, the line Jesus reaches for comes from Psalm thirty-one. It's about the sixth hour, around noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, around three. The sun's light fails. In the temple, the curtain of the sanctuary is torn down the middle. And Jesus, who has been praying all through this Gospel, prays one last time, with a line from the prayers of his people.

In the King James words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd give someone you love into another's care. The psalm reads: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth." Jesus adds one word to the front of it: Father. In Mark and Matthew, his last words from the cross come from a different psalm, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. Luke gives this one instead. Christians keep both, and some hear two sides of the same death: the cry of abandonment, and the word of trust. Then Luke turns to the people watching. A Roman centurion glorifies God and says, "Certainly this was a righteous man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. His friends, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance and watch. Then Joseph, from Arimathea, steps forward: a member of the council who, Luke tells us, hadn't agreed with their decision. He asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut into rock, where no one had ever been laid. The women follow and see where. They go home and prepare spices and ointments. And then, Luke says, they rested on the sabbath, according to the commandment. Even in grief, they keep the sabbath, and wait.
screen: then, large: `INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Think of what you'll carry into bed tonight: your tired body, your worries, the people you love. Imagine opening your hands and placing each one into hands larger than yours, without needing to know how it will turn out. If you pray, you can say it now and again before sleep, into thy hands I commend my spirit; if you don't, simply open your hands on your lap and let the day go.

588.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection every Easter and gather on Sundays because the tomb was found empty on the first day of the week; Orthodox Christians honor the women who came with spices as the Myrrh-bearers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph of Arimathea, a new tomb, and women who rested on the sabbath. Your line: even in grief, keep the sabbath.

Sunday, very early. The sabbath is over. A small group of women set out in the gray light, carrying the spices they prepared, to do the last thing love can do for a body. They know exactly where the tomb is; they watched Joseph lay him there. They are not expecting anything. When they arrive, the stone is already rolled away. They go inside. The body isn't there. Luke says they were much perplexed. And then, suddenly, two men are standing beside them in shining garments.

The women are terrified and bow their faces to the ground. And the two men ask a question, in the King James words: "Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen." Remember what he told you in Galilee, that the Son of man must be delivered, crucified, and rise again the third day. And they remembered his words. Notice who's being reminded: these women had been listening all along. They're disciples, and Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them. They go back and tell the eleven and the rest. And then: "And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not." Idle tales. The Greek word is lēros: nonsense, empty talk. So in Luke the news of the resurrection comes first from women, and the men dismiss it. Luke doesn't hide it. He tells it plainly, and some readers see that plainness as a mark of honesty. Then Peter gets up and runs to the tomb anyway. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not sure yet. Wondering. The women were right first.
screen: then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Think of a time, if there was one, when a woman said something true and wasn't taken seriously, by you or by the people around you: a mother who saw a problem coming, a colleague whose idea went to someone else, a friend told she was overreacting. Hold that memory honestly, and think of one woman whose word you could take more seriously. If you pray, you can give thanks for her.
Leros, the Greek word for nonsense, idle talk: what the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb, when they came with spices for a body that wasn't there.
Your line: he is not here. A week from Peter's tears to Herod, Barabbas, the road, the cross, the tomb, and this question. That's day five hundred eighty-eight, and another week on the path.

original.note: Greek: nonsense, idle talk. Luke's word for how the women's report sounded to the apostles.

chat.says: In Luke, who first brought the news that Jesus was risen?
options: The women, whom Luke names; the men first called their report idle tales.
Peter, who ran to the tomb first and then told the women what he saw.
The Roman guards, who rushed back to the city to report it to Pilate.
chat.meaning: Luke names the women: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James. They told the eleven, and their words seemed as idle tales.
